title: The monarchy divides at Shechem
summary: Rehoboam’s assembly at Shechem ends with the northern tribes rejecting Davidic rule; Jeroboam becomes king over Israel while Judah remains under Rehoboam.
historicalNote: The political division is foundational to the biblical narrative. The conventional date around 930 BCE is a historical reconstruction rather than a date printed in the text.

title: Jeroboam’s Bethel and Dan sanctuaries
summary: Kings associates Jeroboam I with royal cult centers at Bethel and Dan. Both places are mappable; specific ritual installations require site-by-site archaeological interpretation.
historicalNote: Tel Dan preserves major cultic architecture, but assigning every phase or feature directly to Jeroboam I is a chronological interpretation, not an inscribed label.

title: Shoshenq I / biblical Shishak campaigns in the Levant
summary: Kings and Chronicles describe Shishak’s attack during Rehoboam’s reign; Shoshenq I’s Karnak relief independently attests an Egyptian Levantine campaign.
historicalNote: The Shishak–Shoshenq I identification is widely accepted. The Karnak place list is not a transcript of the biblical account and does not simply prove every detail of the Jerusalem narrative.

dating.label: late 10th century BCE; commonly placed around 925 BCE

title: Omri founds Samaria
summary: Omri purchases the hill of Samaria and establishes a new northern capital.
historicalNote: The capital site is secure. Exact regnal-year conversion into BCE depends on chronological system.

title: Battle of Qarqar
summary: Shalmaneser III’s Kurkh Monolith records a major coalition battle at Qarqar and names Ahab of Israel among the coalition. Kings does not narrate this battle.
historicalNote: This is extra-biblical historical context. The Assyrian inscription is a royal victory text; its troop numbers and rhetoric are not treated as neutral statistics.

title: Mesha and Moab rebel against Israel
summary: 2 Kings 3 narrates a coalition campaign against Moab after Mesha rebels. The Mesha Stele independently presents Moabite liberation from Omride domination from a Moabite royal perspective.
historicalNote: The Mesha Stele and 2 Kings overlap in people/political setting but should not be forced into a one-to-one event harmonization.

title: Naboth’s vineyard at Jezreel
summary: 1 Kings 21 places Naboth’s vineyard beside Ahab’s Jezreel property and narrates its seizure through royal abuse.
historicalNote: Jezreel is secure; the vineyard itself is not archaeologically identified.

title: Elijah, drought, Kerith, and Zarephath
summary: The Elijah cycle opens with drought, an unlocated brook east of the Jordan, and a stay in Phoenician Zarephath.
historicalNote: Zarephath is mappable; Kerith is not. The map therefore avoids drawing an exact first leg.

title: Elijah’s confrontation on Mount Carmel
summary: 1 Kings 18 places the contest involving Elijah and prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, followed by rain and movement toward Jezreel.
historicalNote: The Carmel ridge is secure, but the exact altar location and route to Jezreel are not archaeologically traceable.

title: Elijah flees toward Horeb
summary: After the Carmel narrative, Elijah travels via Beersheba into the wilderness and reaches Horeb, “the mountain of God.”
historicalNote: Beersheba is secure; Horeb/Sinai remains unlocated in the atlas, so no exact final route is drawn.

title: Elijah’s departure and Elisha’s succession
summary: 2 Kings 2 moves through Bethel, Jericho, and the Jordan in the transition from Elijah to Elisha.
historicalNote: The named Gilgal in this sequence is not forced onto the Joshua-era Gilgal pin; only better-established anchors are mapped.

title: Naaman washes in the Jordan
summary: 2 Kings 5 places the Aramean commander Naaman in an Israel-Aram diplomatic/prophetic narrative culminating in washing in the Jordan.
historicalNote: The Jordan is a secure physical anchor, but the text does not identify a precise bathing spot. Samaria is included as Northern Kingdom royal-capital context; 2 Kings 5 does not explicitly give a modern coordinate for Elisha’s house.

title: Jehu’s coup reaches Jezreel and Samaria
summary: Jehu is anointed amid the Ramoth-gilead war and rapidly seizes the northern throne, killing Joram and Jezebel at Jezreel before consolidating power in Samaria.
historicalNote: Ramoth-gilead is unlocated, while Jezreel and Samaria are secure. Animation begins from broad Gilead context rather than pretending a precise Ramoth coordinate.

dating.label: mid-9th century BCE; Jehu’s accession conventionally c. 841 BCE

title: Assyrian monument depicts tribute from Jehu
summary: Shalmaneser III’s Black Obelisk includes a tribute scene captioned with Jehu under the Assyrian dynastic label of Omri.
historicalNote: The obelisk was erected later than the tribute episode. “Son/house of Omri” is an Assyrian geopolitical/dynastic label, not a claim that Jehu was Omri’s biological son.

title: Hazael pressures Israel and Judah
summary: Kings portrays Hazael of Damascus taking territory from Israel and later capturing Gath and threatening Jerusalem.
historicalNote: The Tel Dan Stele supplies independent Aramaic royal-war context, but its author and exact event correlations remain debated.

title: Athaliah’s rule and Joash’s accession
summary: The Jerusalem court narrative moves through Athaliah’s seizure of power, Joash’s preservation, and his later public enthronement at the temple.
historicalNote: The Temple Mount is a physical anchor; the exact First Temple spaces involved remain unexcavated/unpinned.

title: Amos confronts the priest of Bethel
summary: Amos 7 places a confrontation between Amos and Amaziah at Bethel, linking a Judean prophet with a northern royal sanctuary.
historicalNote: No route from Tekoa to Bethel is claimed by the text; the map links the places conceptually rather than drawing a journey.

title: Hosea addresses the Northern Kingdom before its fall
summary: Hosea’s oracles repeatedly invoke Ephraim, Israel, Samaria, and Bethel/Beth-aven in the decades of political instability before Assyrian conquest.
historicalNote: The book spans and reflects a complex period; the atlas uses broad late-northern-kingdom context rather than assigning each oracle an exact year.

title: Jonah narrative: Joppa, the sea, and Nineveh
summary: The book of Jonah contrasts an attempted voyage from Joppa toward disputed Tarshish with a divine commission to Nineveh.
historicalNote: Nineveh and Joppa are historical places; Tarshish is disputed. The map visualizes the narrative’s literary geography without using cartography to decide the book’s genre, date of composition, or historicity.

title: Syro-Ephraimite crisis
summary: Rezin of Damascus and Pekah of Israel pressure Judah; Ahaz appeals to Tiglath-pileser III, while Isaiah 7 frames the crisis in Jerusalem.
historicalNote: The wider geopolitical crisis is strongly anchored in Assyrian chronology. The exact Upper Pool/Fuller’s Field meeting place remains unlocated.

title: Tiglath-pileser III annexes northern territories
summary: Assyrian expansion under Tiglath-pileser III captures Damascus and parts of northern Israel; Kings records deportations from Galilee and Transjordan.
historicalNote: Assyrian annals and biblical notices together provide strong chronological context, but exact deportee routes and provincial borders are not reconstructed as surveyed lines.

title: Siege and fall of Samaria
summary: Kings attributes the siege’s beginning to Shalmaneser V and reports Samaria’s capture after three years; Sargon II later claims the conquest and deportation in his own inscriptions.
historicalNote: The end of the Northern Kingdom is historically secure, but the division of credit between Shalmaneser V and Sargon II is debated. The atlas does not hide that historiographic problem.

dating.label: siege/fall around 724–722 BCE; Sargon’s claims continue after accession
dating.note: Exact capture attribution between Shalmaneser V and Sargon II remains debated.

title: Assyrian deportations from the Northern Kingdom
summary: Kings names Halah, the Habor/Khabur region of Gozan, and cities of the Medes as deportation destinations after Samaria’s fall.
historicalNote: The destination list is mappable only in part: Gozan and the Khabur region are secure, Halah is uncertain, and the Median cities are unnamed.

title: Hezekiah’s reform program
summary: Kings and Chronicles associate Hezekiah with centralizing/reforming worship in Judah and removing cultic objects and high places.
historicalNote: Archaeological changes at Judean cult sites are interpreted in multiple ways; they are not all automatically attributed to a single royal decree.

title: Jerusalem waterworks and the Siloam Tunnel
summary: Biblical texts credit Hezekiah with major waterworks; the Siloam Tunnel and its inscription provide a dramatic archaeological context for Iron Age Jerusalem engineering.
historicalNote: The physical tunnel is certain; the inscription does not name Hezekiah. The atlas therefore separates archaeological feature from royal attribution.

title: Sennacherib captures Lachish
summary: In 701 BCE the Assyrian army captures Lachish. Archaeology, Assyrian reliefs, inscriptions, and biblical references converge unusually strongly on this event.
historicalNote: The siege of Lachish is one of the strongest archaeological-textual correlations in the atlas. Assyrian palace reliefs depict the capture; excavation confirms a violent destruction horizon and siege works.

title: Sennacherib’s 701 BCE pressure on Jerusalem
summary: Biblical narratives describe Assyrian demands and Jerusalem’s deliverance. Sennacherib’s annals report devastating Judah and confining Hezekiah in Jerusalem while claiming tribute, but do not claim the city’s capture.
historicalNote: The historical campaign and Jerusalem’s non-capture are strongly supported. The miraculous and theological dimensions of the biblical account are presented as Scripture, not as archaeologically testable claims.

title: Micah’s Shephelah and Jerusalem horizon
summary: Micah 1 names a chain of towns in Judah’s Shephelah and addresses both Samaria and Jerusalem in the shadow of imperial crisis.
historicalNote: Several Micah 1 wordplays depend on place names whose exact modern identifications vary; the atlas does not manufacture points for uncertain towns.
